analysis.one_liner: Gives workers stronger tools to recover wages employers stole from them.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single vote or hearing; every wage-violation penalty, paystub rule, and grant program it proposed never advanced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would crack down on 'wage theft' — when employers don't pay workers everything they've earned, by skipping minimum wage, denying overtime, requiring off-the-clock work, misclassifying workers, or withholding tips. It would require employers to tell workers their pay rate and classification, give detailed paystubs, and pay final wages within 14 days of leaving a job. It would roughly triple the damages workers can recover, extend the deadline to sue from 2 to 4 years, stop employers from forcing workers into arbitration to waive those claims, and fund community groups that help workers recover unpaid wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers underpay them — especially low-wage workers in restaurants, retail, construction, janitorial, and agriculture, where studies cited in the bill find violations affect most workers in a given week. Women, immigrants, and Black workers, who experience minimum wage violations at higher rates, would benefit disproportionately. Law-abiding employers would also gain, since noncompliant competitors could no longer undercut them by skirting payroll.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal right to be paid the actual contract wage (not just the legal minimum), plus paystub and disclosure requirements so workers can see how their pay was calculated, in their primary language
Requires final pay within 14 days of leaving a job, with daily pay for late payment, and lets workers demand up to 5 years of their own payroll records within 21 days

Raises recoverable damages to double unpaid wages plus interest (triple in retaliation cases), extends the time to sue from 2 years to 4 (5 for willful violations), and bars employers from forcing employees to sign away these court rights in arbitration agreements

Raises civil fines to $22,030 per affected employee per violation ($110,150 for repeat or willful violations), makes record-falsification by repeat offenders an automatic criminal referral, and authorizes $50 million a year in grants to community groups that help workers recover unpaid wages

analysis.who_pays: Employers who underpay or violate recordkeeping rules, who would face higher damages, fines, and litigation exposure; compliant employers would bear modest new costs to produce disclosures and paystubs.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on all employers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act: new paystub, disclosure, and 14-day final-pay rules add administrative work, and small businesses with honest payroll practices would feel the paperwork burden alongside violators

Doubling and tripling damages plus a doubled statute of limitations would substantially raise litigation exposure for businesses, and critics of such provisions argue this invites lawsuits beyond genuine wage theft cases

The grant program would spend $50 million in federal money per year through fiscal 2027, flowing partly to labor unions and advocacy groups, which opponents would characterize as funding allied organizations with taxpayer dollars

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core problem the bill targets is real and well-documented in its own findings: workers lose an estimated $15 billion a year to wage violations, and in some industries fewer than half of employers comply with wage law. The main costs are administrative and fall hardest on small businesses that must build new paystub and disclosure systems. The heavier penalties and longer lawsuit window are the point — the bill's findings argue current penalties are too light to deter repeat violators — but they would also raise legal risk for employers generally. Whether the compliance costs outweigh the recovered wages depends largely on how often a given employer underpays its workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Wage Theft Prevention and Wage Recovery Act on September 12, 2023, with nine original cosponsors
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce
Eighteen House members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats; no Republican signed on
The committee took no further action — no markup, no hearing on the bill, no vote — and the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 with the bill never reported out

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who underpay workers are better off, since the penalties, damages, disclosure rules, and grant-funded enforcement that would have applied to them never took effect. Workers left with $15 billion in unpaid wages a year remain where they were.

for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill; all were Democrats

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill never advanced past referral to the Republican-chaired committee.

industries.industry: Employers in low-wage industries (restaurants, retail, janitorial, construction, agriculture)
industries.note: These employers are where wage violations concentrate — the bill's findings cite compliance below 50% in some industries. They would face triple damages, per-employee fines up to $110,150 for repeat violations, mandatory paystubs and disclosures, and community-group monitoring.
The bill would bar employers from using arbitration clauses to waive workers' rights to sue collectively for stolen wages, closing a common shield against wage claims.
Honest employers would gain a level playing field against noncompliant competitors but would bear new paystub, disclosure, and 14-day final-pay compliance costs.
